note: 24 Western + 24 cross-cultural (DRAFT). Human baseline exists only for the 12 has_human_baseline scenarios. Cross-cultural scenarios are model-only/exploratory and not for paper claims.

pole_b.label: Autonomous
pole_b.description: Individual is the primary moral unit

pole_b.label: Skeptical
pole_b.description: Authority must be earned and justified

pole_a.label: Broad
pole_a.description: Morality includes purity, loyalty, dignity, duty

pole_b.label: Narrow
pole_b.description: Morality covers harm and fairness only

scenarios.stimulus: A young woman receives a significant job offer in another city. Her mother has recently been diagnosed with a serious illness and needs ongoing support. She turns down the job to stay close to home.

judgment.question: How do you see her decision?

options.text: She fulfilled a moral obligation to her family
Her own goals and growth matter too — staying may not have been the right choice for her
This was a personal decision about priorities, not a moral one

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding her decision?

options.text: Family obligations come before personal ambition
She would carry guilt or regret if she left
Others in her life would judge her for leaving

scenarios.stimulus: A first-generation college student is offered a place in a prestigious graduate program abroad. His extended family made significant financial sacrifices to support his education, expecting him to return home after graduation to help support his younger siblings and contribute to the family business. He accepts the program.

judgment.question: How do you see his decision?

options.text: He put personal ambition ahead of his responsibilities
He faced a genuine conflict — both paths had legitimate claims on him
He exercised his right to shape his own future

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding his decision?

options.text: Family members have a right to count on each other
Education ultimately serves the whole family, even if it takes time
Each person must decide their own path regardless of expectations

scenarios.stimulus: A team lead is offered a promotion that would move her to a different division. Her current team, which she built and mentored over three years, will likely be reassigned to a manager they find difficult. She accepts the promotion.

judgment.question: How do you see her decision?

options.text: She is abandoning people who depended on her
She earned the opportunity and her team will adapt
She should have made sure her team was taken care of before leaving

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding her decision?

options.text: Three years of mentorship creates a bond that doesn’t end when a better offer arrives.
Staying out of guilt helps no one and sets a precedent that traps good people.
The measure of a leader is what happens to the team after they leave.

scenarios.stimulus: A researcher develops a breakthrough idea while working on a team project. The idea came entirely from her own late-night work, but it builds on the team's shared foundation. She must decide whether to publish it as a solo paper or include the full team as co-authors.

judgment.question: How should she handle authorship?

options.text: She should include the team. The work grew from shared soil.
She should publish solo. The idea was hers.
She should offer co-authorship to those who directly contributed, not the whole team.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this decision?

options.text: Individual contributions exist within a web of relationships that made them possible.
Intellectual honesty requires crediting the person who did the work.
Fair attribution means tracing the actual chain of contribution.

scenarios.stimulus: A father discovers that his teenage son was involved in vandalizing a neighbor's property along with several other boys. The neighbor doesn't know which boys were responsible. The father is considering whether to insist his son confess, knowing it will result in consequences for his son while the other boys go unpunished.

judgment.question: How do you see the father's situation?

options.text: He should insist his son come forward. A parent owes it to the child, to himself, and to the community to raise a person of integrity.
Whether to confess should be his son's own decision. Moral agency cannot be imposed.
He should guide his son but ultimately let him choose.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Raising a good person is a relational obligation that connects parent, child, and community.
Each person must develop their own moral compass, even through mistakes.
Repairing the harm matters more than how accountability happens.

scenarios.stimulus: A young man from a tight-knit fishing community wants to become an artist. His family and community see this as rejecting who they are and what they stand for. He is not abandoning anyone; he plans to stay in the community. But pursuing art means defining himself differently than his community defines him.

judgment.question: How do you see his choice?

options.text: He is rejecting something meaningful about his people by redefining himself.
He has every right to define who he is regardless of where he comes from.
He can honor his roots and still choose his own path.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding his choice?

options.text: Who we are is shaped by the people and place we come from.
Identity is something each person constructs for themselves.
A person can belong to a community without being defined by it.

scenarios.stimulus: A teacher ignores a new school policy she believes harms her students and continues teaching as before.

judgment.question: How do you see her decision?

options.text: Her professional judgment should override the policy
Institutional rules must be followed even when individuals disagree
The outcome for students matters more than whether she followed the rule

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding her decision?

options.text: Professionals have a duty to use their own judgment when they see harm
Rules exist to protect everyone equally, even when imperfect
The well-being of those affected should determine what’s right
Authority deserves the benefit of the doubt

scenarios.stimulus: A junior employee discovers that a company procedure she was told to follow is producing inaccurate results. Her manager tells her to keep following the procedure until leadership reviews it. She quietly corrects the errors on her own.

judgment.question: How do you see her decision?

options.text: She did the right thing by fixing what she knew was wrong
She should have followed her manager’s instruction and waited
Her intent was good but going around her manager creates other problems

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding her decision?

options.text: Accuracy matters more than following a chain of command
Organizations depend on people respecting established processes
She should have escalated rather than acted alone
A manager’s instructions should be followed unless clearly unethical

scenarios.stimulus: A community elder makes a decision about a local dispute that several younger members believe is unfair. The elder’s authority has traditionally been respected without question in this community.

judgment.question: How do you see the situation?

options.text: The younger members should speak up if the decision is unjust
Respecting the elder’s authority preserves something valuable in the community
Both the elder’s wisdom and the younger members’ concerns deserve consideration

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this situation?

options.text: No one’s authority should be beyond challenge
Traditional authority carries earned wisdom that outsiders may not see
Fairness matters more than tradition

scenarios.stimulus: A small town must decide whether to approve a new water treatment method. The town's engineers unanimously recommend it as significantly safer. A majority of residents oppose it after reading online articles raising concerns the engineers say are unfounded.

judgment.question: How should the town proceed?

options.text: The engineers' expertise should carry the decision.
The residents' democratic voice should be respected even if the experts disagree.
The town should invest more time in helping residents understand the science before deciding.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this decision?

options.text: Technical decisions should be made by people with technical knowledge.
Legitimacy comes from the consent of the people affected, not from credentials.
Good decisions require both expertise and public trust.

scenarios.stimulus: A woman has been part of a religious community for twenty years. Her spiritual leader instructs members to cut ties with family members who have left the faith. She deeply respects her leader and believes in the community's teachings, but the instruction troubles her.

judgment.question: How should she respond?

options.text: She should follow her leader's guidance. She chose this path and its authority.
She should trust her own conscience over any leader's instruction.
She should seek dialogue with the leader rather than simply obeying or refusing.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Committing to a spiritual path means accepting its authority, even when it is hard.
No authority, chosen or not, should override a person's moral judgment.
Healthy authority allows questioning without demanding obedience.

scenarios.stimulus: A doctor believes a patient would benefit from an unconventional treatment. Every colleague she consults disagrees, citing standard protocols and the lack of published evidence for her approach. She has seen it work in two previous cases.

judgment.question: How should she proceed?

options.text: She should defer to her colleagues' consensus and follow standard protocols.
Her direct experience with patients should carry more weight than colleagues' theoretical objections.
She should document her reasoning and seek a formal review rather than acting alone.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this decision?

options.text: Medical consensus exists to protect patients from individual doctors' biases.
A doctor's primary obligation is to the patient in front of her, not to protocols.
Established processes for challenging consensus exist for good reason.

scenarios.stimulus: A man spends most weekends on a solitary hobby that some of his neighbors consider improper. No one has been injured or lost money because of it, but several neighbors have spoken to him directly about their concerns.

judgment.question: How do you see the situation?

options.text: The neighbors are right to hold him accountable to community standards
What he does privately is outside the scope of anyone else’s moral concern
This is a matter of social preference, not morality — the neighbors may dislike it, but that doesn’t make it wrong

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this situation?

options.text: A community has the right to uphold shared standards of behavior
Private behavior that doesn’t affect others is outside the moral domain
Discomfort is not the same as a moral violation — people can disapprove without being wronged

scenarios.stimulus: A family member consistently refuses to participate in important cultural or religious traditions that the rest of the family observes. No one is harmed by the refusal, but other family members feel it shows a lack of respect.

judgment.question: How do you see the situation?

options.text: Refusing to participate in family traditions is a form of disrespect that matters morally
Participation in traditions is a personal choice, not a moral obligation
The family’s feelings are understandable, but no one can be compelled to observe traditions

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this situation?

options.text: Shared traditions hold families together and refusing weakens the bond
Religious and cultural practice must be freely chosen to be meaningful
Respect for family can be shown in ways other than participating in specific rituals

scenarios.stimulus: A restaurant in a traditional neighborhood begins serving food that many longtime residents consider disrespectful to local customs and values. No health or safety issues have been raised.

judgment.question: How do you see the situation?

options.text: The restaurant should respect the neighborhood’s established customs
A business can serve whatever it chooses — customers will decide with their wallets
The residents’ concerns are worth hearing, but a business has no obligation to conform

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this situation?

options.text: Neighborhoods have a character worth preserving and newcomers should respect it
In a free society, businesses operate by market rules, not community approval
Dialogue between the restaurant and residents is more productive than moral judgment

scenarios.stimulus: A wealthy man hires people from a low-income neighborhood to perform humiliating but legal tasks for entertainment at his private parties. The workers are paid well, participate voluntarily, and report no complaints. No one outside the parties knows about it.

judgment.question: How do you see this?

options.text: This is morally wrong regardless of consent. There are limits to what can be bought, even voluntarily.
If the workers consent and are paid fairly, it is their choice to make.
It is distasteful but not a moral issue as long as no one is coerced.

reasoning.question: What matters most in evaluating this?

options.text: Some exchanges cross a moral line even when both parties agree to them.
Consenting adults have the right to make their own choices about what they are willing to do.
The power imbalance makes genuine consent questionable.

scenarios.stimulus: A family continues to buy products from a company widely reported to use exploitative labor practices overseas. The family is aware of the reports but says the products are the best value for their budget and they are not personally responsible for a company's overseas operations.

judgment.question: How do you see their choice?

options.text: Knowingly supporting exploitation through purchases is a moral failure.
Consumers are not responsible for supply chains they did not create.
It is worth considering but individual purchases don't meaningfully change corporate behavior.

reasoning.question: What matters most in evaluating their choice?

options.text: Morality extends to the consequences of our economic choices, even indirect ones.
People have a right to make purchasing decisions based on their own family's needs.
Systemic problems require systemic solutions, not individual guilt.

scenarios.stimulus: At a private dinner with close friends, a man tells jokes that mock a vulnerable group. No members of that group are present. His friends laugh but one later feels uncomfortable about having laughed.

judgment.question: How do you see this?

options.text: Even in private, mocking vulnerable people is morally wrong.
What people say among friends in private is not a moral matter.
It reflects poor character but is not the same as causing harm.

reasoning.question: What matters most in evaluating this?

options.text: Dehumanizing people in private normalizes it and makes it easier for others to do the same.
The moral domain covers actions that affect others, not private speech among consenting adults.
Intent and context matter. The same words carry different moral weight in different settings.

scenarios.stimulus: After a natural disaster, a local organization has enough supplies for only half the affected families and must decide how to distribute them.

judgment.question: How should the supplies be distributed?

options.text: Those closest to the organization should receive help first
Those in greatest need should receive help first
Everyone affected deserves equal consideration regardless of connection

reasoning.question: What matters most in making this decision?

options.text: You owe the most to those you know and have relationships with
Severity of need is the only morally relevant criterion
Fairness requires equal treatment regardless of relationship
The community’s long-term survival depends on protecting the most vulnerable

scenarios.stimulus: A manager has one remaining spot on a high-visibility project. A close colleague who is reasonably qualified has asked to be considered. A person from another department whom the manager barely knows is clearly the strongest candidate.

judgment.question: How should the manager decide?

options.text: Loyalty to a colleague who asked for help should carry real weight
The most qualified person should get the spot, period
Both relationship and qualification matter — the manager should weigh them honestly

reasoning.question: What matters most in making this decision?

options.text: Ignoring someone who trusted you enough to ask damages the fabric of a team.
If word gets out that connections matter more than skill, it poisons the whole system.
The right answer depends on how large the qualification gap actually is.

scenarios.stimulus: A family learns that a distant relative they have never met is in serious financial difficulty. Helping would require a meaningful sacrifice from the family’s own savings.

judgment.question: What should the family do?

options.text: Family is family — they should help even if they’ve never met
They have no real obligation to a stranger who happens to share a name
They should help if they can, but the sacrifice shouldn’t be expected

reasoning.question: What matters most in making this decision?

options.text: If family doesn’t help family, the whole safety net unravels.
You can’t owe someone a meaningful sacrifice when you don’t even know their name.
Helping is admirable, but making it expected turns generosity into guilt.

scenarios.stimulus: A teacher has limited time for after-school tutoring. She can spend all her time with one struggling student who needs intensive help to pass, or she can spread her time across five students who would each benefit moderately.

judgment.question: How should she decide?

options.text: Focus on the one student. The deepest need deserves the fullest response.
Spread the time. Helping five students moderately does more total good.
Consider which students she knows best and has the strongest relationship with.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this decision?

options.text: We owe the most to those in the greatest need, even if it means others get less.
Five students helped moderately adds up to more total benefit than one student helped deeply.
A teacher's first obligation is to the students she knows personally.

scenarios.stimulus: A woman is rushing to pick up her four-year-old from daycare before it closes. She sees a stranger on the sidewalk who has fallen and appears to be in pain but is conscious and not in danger. Stopping to help would mean her daughter waits alone at daycare past closing time, which has happened before and frightened the child.

judgment.question: How should she respond?

options.text: Her daughter comes first. She should keep going.
She should stop and help. A person in pain right in front of you takes priority.
She should make a quick assessment and call for help if she cannot stop.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Your first obligation is always to the people closest to you.
Proximity creates obligation. When you see someone suffering, you owe them a response.
Everyone deserves help regardless of whether you know them.

scenarios.stimulus: A small coastal town must decide whether to spend its limited budget on improving current residents' services or on building sea walls that will primarily benefit people who live there decades from now. Current residents would see little personal benefit from the sea walls during their lifetimes.

judgment.question: How should the town decide?

options.text: Current residents' needs should take priority. They are the ones paying.
Future residents deserve protection even if current residents bear the cost.
The town should balance both but give some weight to the people who are here now.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this decision?

options.text: We owe the most to the community we live in now.
Moral obligation extends to people who will be affected by our choices, even if they don't exist yet.
Good stewardship means thinking beyond the current generation.

scenarios.tradition_note: Ubuntu personhood: 'umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu' (a person is a person through other persons). Personhood is achieved through moral conduct within community, not given at birth. The dilemma: what happens when the community's definition of moral conduct conflicts with what the person believes is right?
scenarios.stimulus: A woman in a close-knit community has developed skills as a healer through years of working alongside her grandmother. Community members come to her for help. She has also been accepted into a formal medical training program that would take her away for several years. Her community tells her she is already a healer — leaving to study elsewhere suggests their ways are not enough. She believes formal training would let her help more people, including her own community.

judgment.question: How do you see her situation?

options.text: She is who she is because of her community. Leaving to become something else elsewhere diminishes that.
She should pursue the training that lets her grow, even if the community does not understand.
She can honor what her community gave her and still seek to become more.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding her situation?

options.text: Leaving says the community's knowledge is not enough. That judgment wounds the people who taught her.
Growth sometimes requires leaving, and a community that cannot accept that is holding her back.
True belonging allows a person to grow without it being seen as rejection.

scenarios.tradition_note: Confucian self-cultivation through the five relationships (wu lun). The self is defined by and through relationships, especially parent-child. The dilemma: when fulfilling one relationship requires failing another.
scenarios.stimulus: A man's aging parents expect him to take over the family's traditional craft workshop, as the eldest son has done for five generations. His wife and children live in a city where the children are thriving in school. Moving the family back would uproot his children's education and his wife's career. Staying means the workshop closes and the family tradition ends with his father.

judgment.question: How do you see his situation?

options.text: His first obligation is to his parents and the continuity of the family line.
His obligation to his wife and children's future is just as real and more immediate.
He must find his own answer. No tradition can tell a person which family to fail.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding his situation?

options.text: Five generations of tradition carry moral weight that one person's preferences cannot override.
A father's duty to his children's wellbeing is no less binding than a son's duty to his parents.
Each person must weigh these obligations for themselves — no formula resolves them.

scenarios.tradition_note: Svadharma: each person has a dharma (moral duty) specific to their role, stage of life, and nature. The dilemma: when personal nature (svabhava) pulls toward a dharma the family and community do not recognize.
scenarios.stimulus: A young man from a family of merchants feels called to a life of study and teaching. His family sees this as abandoning his duty — the family business supports not just them but employees and their families who depend on it. He does not reject his family. He believes his nature draws him to a different kind of service. His father says that duty is not something you choose based on what feels right; it is given to you by your circumstances.

judgment.question: How do you see his situation?

options.text: His father is right. Duty comes from your place in the world, not from personal preference.
Following one's own nature is itself a duty. A life lived against one's nature serves no one well.
Both claims are real. The question is which duty weighs more in his particular circumstances.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding his situation?

options.text: Duty is given by one's position and relationships, not chosen by desire.
A person who ignores their own nature will fulfill their assigned role poorly.
The people who depend on the business have a claim that personal calling does not erase.

scenarios.tradition_note: The individual as khalifah (steward/trustee) before God. Personal moral agency is real but exercised within the framework of ummah (community) and divine purpose. The dilemma: when individual conscience points away from community practice.
scenarios.stimulus: A woman has studied her faith deeply and has come to interpret certain religious obligations differently than her local community does. Her interpretation is shared by respected scholars in other regions but is considered incorrect by the scholars her community follows. She begins practicing according to her own understanding. Her family says she is placing her individual judgment above the community's collective wisdom.

judgment.question: How do you see her decision?

options.text: Faith is ultimately between the individual and God. She has studied and reached her own understanding.
The community's shared understanding carries wisdom that individual study may miss.
Both individual study and communal tradition have authority. She should seek dialogue, not simply diverge.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding her decision?

options.text: Each person is accountable for their own faith. No community can stand between a person and their understanding of truth.
Generations of communal scholarship protect against the errors of individual reasoning.
Scholarly disagreement is normal. What matters is that she engaged seriously, not that she reached a different conclusion.

scenarios.tradition_note: Ubuntu achieved personhood: you become a full person through your moral relationships and contributions to community. The dilemma: what does the community owe someone who has contributed but is now in need?
scenarios.stimulus: An older man who spent decades mediating disputes, mentoring young people, and contributing to communal work has fallen ill and can no longer contribute. Some younger community members suggest that resources should go to those who are still actively contributing. Others say the community owes him everything — he helped make them who they are.

judgment.question: How do you see this situation?

options.text: The community is obligated to care for him. He is part of who they are.
Resources should go where they do the most good for the community now.
Care for elders and practical needs both matter. The community should find a way to honor both.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: A community that abandons the people who built it destroys the very thing that makes it a community.
Sentiment cannot override the practical reality of limited resources.
How a community treats those who can no longer contribute reveals its true character.

scenarios.tradition_note: Ren (humaneness/benevolence) as cultivated through proper relationships. The dilemma: when self-cultivation conflicts with relational harmony.
scenarios.stimulus: A woman has been offered a position that would let her use her talents fully, but accepting would mean publicly surpassing her older brother, who holds a similar but less prominent role in the same field. In their family, the eldest sibling's position has always been respected. Her brother has not asked her to decline, but she knows accepting would cause him to lose face.

judgment.question: How do you see her situation?

options.text: Preserving her brother's dignity and the family's harmony matters more than her advancement.
Her talents are her own. Using them fully is not an insult to anyone.
She should accept but find ways to honor her brother's position publicly.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding her situation?

options.text: Relationships are maintained through awareness of each person's position and dignity.
A family that requires its members to diminish themselves is not practicing real harmony.
True respect means navigating advancement without humiliation, not avoiding advancement.

scenarios.tradition_note: Xiao (filial piety): children owe deep respect and obedience to parents, but the Analects also recognizes gentle remonstrance when a parent errs. The dilemma: when does filial respect require silence and when does it require speaking?
scenarios.stimulus: An adult son discovers that his widowed father has been giving a large portion of the family's savings to a religious organization that the son believes is exploiting him. The father finds deep meaning and community in his involvement. Confronting his father would be seen as deeply disrespectful — questioning both his judgment and his faith. Remaining silent means watching the family's financial security disappear.

judgment.question: How should the son respond?

options.text: He must speak, even at the cost of disrespecting his father. Protecting his father from harm is itself an act of devotion.
His father is an adult whose choices deserve respect, even when the son disagrees. To override him would be arrogant.
He should express his concern gently and privately, then accept whatever his father decides.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: A child who truly honors a parent will protect them even when it means disagreeing.
Respect for a parent's autonomy and dignity is not conditional on agreeing with their choices.
There is a way to express concern that preserves respect. That is the path to follow.

scenarios.tradition_note: Ijma (scholarly consensus) and shura (consultation) as sources of authority. Individual ijtihad (independent reasoning) is recognized but bounded. The dilemma: when established scholarly consensus may not address a genuinely new situation.
scenarios.stimulus: A community faces a new ethical question that existing scholarly rulings do not directly address. The senior scholars in the community apply an older ruling by analogy and declare the matter settled. A younger scholar argues that the analogy does not hold and that independent reasoning is needed because the situation is genuinely unprecedented. The senior scholars say that reopening settled methodology creates confusion and weakens the community's coherence.

judgment.question: How should the community proceed?

options.text: The senior scholars' experience and the weight of tradition should prevail.
The younger scholar is right to insist on fresh reasoning for a genuinely new situation.
The community should convene a broader consultation rather than letting either side simply declare the answer.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Centuries of accumulated wisdom are not overturned because one person sees things differently.
Applying old answers to new problems without examination is not faithfulness — it is rigidity.
The process of consultation itself is more important than which scholar prevails.

scenarios.tradition_note: Guru-shishya (teacher-disciple) relationship: the guru's authority is based on spiritual realization and lineage. The dilemma: when the guru's teaching conflicts with the disciple's direct experience.
scenarios.stimulus: A devoted student has studied under a respected teacher for many years. The teacher instructs all students to follow a specific spiritual practice. The student has practiced it faithfully but finds that a different practice, one the teacher has explicitly discouraged, produces the spiritual growth the student has been seeking. The teacher says that students cannot judge their own progress — that is precisely why they need a guide.

judgment.question: How should the student respond?

options.text: The teacher's authority comes from deeper knowledge. The student should trust the teacher's judgment over his own experience.
Spiritual practice must ultimately be validated by one's own experience. No teacher can overrule that.
He should share his experience honestly with the teacher and see what emerges from the conversation.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: A teacher who has walked the path further can see what the student cannot yet see.
The purpose of all teaching is to develop the student's own discernment, not permanent dependence.
The relationship between teacher and student is itself the practice — how they navigate disagreement matters.

scenarios.tradition_note: Indaba (communal deliberation): authority is vested in the process of collective discussion, not in any single leader. But the process requires that certain voices carry more weight. The dilemma: when the consensus process is being used to silence legitimate dissent.
scenarios.stimulus: A community council is deliberating about allocating farmland. The council's tradition is to discuss until consensus is reached. Several women in the community argue that the proposed allocation is unfair to families headed by women. The council elders, all men, say the women's concerns have been heard but that consensus has been reached. The women say that consensus was reached by excluding their voices from the final discussion.

judgment.question: How do you see this situation?

options.text: The council's process must be respected. Consensus is consensus, even when some disagree.
A consensus that excludes affected voices is not real consensus. The women are right to challenge it.
The process failed here. The right response is to fix the process, not to override the council.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Communal decision-making depends on respecting the process, even when the outcome is imperfect.
A process that systematically excludes some voices has no moral authority.
The strength of communal deliberation is that it can correct itself. This is that moment.

scenarios.tradition_note: Amr bil-maruf (commanding the good) and the tension between personal conscience and communal religious authority. The dilemma: who has the standing to interpret and enforce moral obligations?
scenarios.stimulus: A successful businesswoman runs her company according to ethical principles she derives from her faith. A local religious leader publicly criticizes her practices, saying that her interpretation of ethical business is too liberal and that she is setting a bad example. She believes her approach is well-grounded in her own study. The religious leader has significant influence in the community where most of her employees and customers live.

judgment.question: How should she respond?

options.text: A religious leader's public guidance should be taken seriously. She should reconsider her practices.
She has done her own study and her conscience is clear. She should continue as she believes is right.
She should engage the leader in private dialogue rather than either submitting or publicly defying him.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Religious leaders carry a responsibility to guide the community, and that role deserves deference.
Each person is ultimately responsible for their own moral choices before God.
Public disagreement between respected community members harms everyone. Resolution should happen privately.

scenarios.tradition_note: Shastra (scriptural authority) vs. anubhava (lived experience). Hindu tradition recognizes both but debates their relative weight. The dilemma: when inherited practice conflicts with contemporary moral intuition.
scenarios.stimulus: A family has observed specific ancestral rituals for generations. A young woman in the family, educated in both traditional texts and modern ethics, argues that one of the rituals reinforces a social hierarchy that the family should no longer perpetuate. Her grandmother says the ritual connects them to their ancestors and that changing it severs something that cannot be repaired. The ritual does not cause direct harm but it symbolically elevates some family members above others.

judgment.question: How do you see her challenge?

options.text: The ritual connects the family to something larger than the present moment. Changing it for contemporary values risks losing something irreplaceable.
A practice that reinforces hierarchy should be changed, regardless of how long it has been observed.
The family should discuss it together. Neither unquestioning continuation nor unilateral change is right.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Inherited practices carry wisdom and meaning that may not be visible to those who want to change them.
Every generation has the right and duty to examine what it inherits and keep only what is just.
The meaning of a ritual can evolve without the ritual being abandoned.

scenarios.tradition_note: Shuddhi/ashuddhi (purity/impurity) as a moral category, not just a hygiene category. Certain actions, foods, and associations carry moral weight beyond their physical effects. The dilemma: is purity a legitimate moral concern or a social control mechanism?
scenarios.stimulus: A family is preparing for an important religious ceremony. A family member who recently returned from abroad has been eating food the family considers impure — not harmful, but outside the boundaries of what their tradition permits. The family asks him to observe dietary restrictions for a period before participating in the ceremony. He says the food caused no harm and that the restrictions are arbitrary.

judgment.question: How do you see this situation?

options.text: The dietary restrictions carry real moral and spiritual weight. He should observe them out of respect for the ceremony and his family.
If the food caused no harm, the restrictions are social customs, not moral obligations.
He should observe them for the sake of family harmony, even if he personally disagrees about their importance.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this situation?

options.text: Purity is a moral category, not just a physical one. Some boundaries matter even when no visible harm is done.
Morality is about harm and fairness. Dietary rules that cause no harm belong to personal preference, not ethics.
The family's shared practice deserves respect as a practice, regardless of whether the individual finds it meaningful.

scenarios.tradition_note: Halal/haram framework: the moral domain explicitly extends to categories of consumption, dress, and social interaction that Western liberal ethics treats as personal preference. The dilemma: when the framework is applied to others who do not share it.
scenarios.stimulus: A family runs a small restaurant. They have always operated according to their faith's dietary laws. A new employee, who does not share their faith, eats food during working hours that violates those laws — not in the restaurant, but in the break room. The family feels this is disrespectful to the space they have created. The employee says what he eats on his break is his own business.

judgment.question: How do you see this situation?

options.text: The family has the right to maintain the moral character of their space, including the break room.
What an employee eats on a break is a personal matter, not a moral one the employer can govern.
Both have legitimate concerns. A practical compromise is better than a moral standoff.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this situation?

options.text: A space created according to moral principles is diminished when those principles are violated within it.
Imposing dietary rules on someone who does not share the underlying beliefs crosses a line.
Employment creates mutual obligations. Both sides should have discussed expectations from the start.

scenarios.tradition_note: Ubuntu moral domain: individual behavior that disrupts communal harmony is a moral matter even if no individual is directly harmed. The category of 'harmless private behavior' barely exists in strong communitarian ethics.
scenarios.stimulus: A man in a close-knit village has acquired considerably more wealth than his neighbors through legitimate means. Rather than sharing in customary ways — hosting community meals, contributing to collective projects, supporting families in need — he has built a large private house and keeps largely to himself. No one has been cheated or harmed. But the visible inequality and his withdrawal from communal life are creating resentment and division.

judgment.question: How do you see his behavior?

options.text: He is violating a moral obligation. Wealth creates duties to the community that produced the conditions for his success.
He earned his wealth honestly. How he spends it is his own affair.
His behavior is selfish but not immoral. The community can disapprove without claiming he owes them.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this situation?

options.text: In a community, individual success that is not shared corrodes the bonds that make everyone's life possible.
A person's property and choices about it are not subject to communal moral claims.
The resentment is real but the solution is dialogue, not declaring his choices immoral.

scenarios.tradition_note: Li (ritual propriety): proper conduct in relationships — forms of address, posture, gift-giving, ceremony — carries genuine moral weight, not just social weight. The dilemma: when li feels empty but is still morally demanded.
scenarios.stimulus: A grandson is expected to perform elaborate mourning rituals for his grandfather, who he barely knew. The rituals require weeks of observance that will affect his work and family life. He did not have a close relationship with his grandfather and feels the rituals would be performative rather than genuine. His family says the rituals are not about his personal feelings — they are about honoring the relationship itself and maintaining the moral order of the family.

judgment.question: How do you see his situation?

options.text: The rituals honor the relationship and the family's continuity. His personal feelings are not the point.
Performing rituals without genuine feeling is empty and possibly dishonest.
He should participate in a way that honors his family without pretending to grief he does not feel.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding his situation?

options.text: Ritual maintains moral order. Its value does not depend on the performer's personal emotions.
Actions without authentic feeling behind them teach a person to perform virtue rather than practice it.
The question is not whether to observe the ritual but how to do so honestly.

scenarios.tradition_note: Haya (modesty/dignity): modesty in dress and behavior is a moral category, not merely aesthetic or personal. The dilemma: when modesty norms are applied across different contexts and generations.
scenarios.stimulus: A young woman dresses modestly by her own standards but not by her grandmother's. Her grandmother says modesty is not a matter of personal interpretation — it has clear moral requirements that reflect one's relationship with God and community. The granddaughter says she respects the principle of modesty but expresses it differently than previous generations did. Neither is questioning the other's faith.

judgment.question: How do you see this disagreement?

options.text: Modesty has standards that are not up to individual reinterpretation. The grandmother's understanding reflects the tradition more faithfully.
Modesty is a principle, not a dress code. Each generation can express it authentically in its own way.
Both are sincere in their faith. The disagreement is about cultural expression, not moral substance.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding this disagreement?

options.text: Moral principles require specific practices. Without concrete standards, the principle dissolves into whatever anyone wants it to mean.
Clinging to one generation's expression of a principle confuses the form with the substance.
What matters is the sincerity of practice, not its external form.

scenarios.tradition_note: Pitru-dharma (ancestral obligations): duties to ancestors — rituals, remembrance, continuing lineage — are moral obligations, not optional observances. The dilemma: when ancestral obligations conflict with contemporary life choices.
scenarios.stimulus: A couple has decided not to have children. In their family's tradition, continuing the family line is a moral duty owed to one's ancestors — not just a personal preference but an obligation that connects the living to those who came before. The couple's parents are deeply distressed, saying the couple is breaking a chain of obligation that stretches back generations. The couple says they can honor their ancestors in other ways.

judgment.question: How do you see the couple's decision?

options.text: The obligation to continue the family line is real and not theirs to set aside unilaterally.
Having children is a personal decision. Framing it as a moral duty to the dead is an imposition on the living.
The obligation is meaningful but can be honored in ways other than biological continuation.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding their decision?

options.text: We owe something to those who came before us. That debt is not canceled by modern ideas about personal choice.
Obligations to the dead cannot override the living's right to make their own life choices.
The principle of honoring ancestors is valid; the specific form it takes can change with circumstances.

scenarios.tradition_note: Concentric circles of obligation in Ubuntu: family first, then extended family, then community, then strangers. But ubuntu also says 'a person is a person through other persons' — which implies no person is truly a stranger.
scenarios.stimulus: A village has a well that produces enough water for its own families with some to spare. People from a neighboring village, displaced by drought, arrive asking to share the well. Sharing means rationing for everyone. Some villagers say their first obligation is to their own families and that rationing risks their children's health. Others say turning away people in need would make the village something less than a community.

judgment.question: How should the village decide?

options.text: The village's own families come first. You cannot help others by putting your own children at risk.
Turning away people in desperate need is a moral failure regardless of the cost to the village.
Share, but with limits that protect both communities. Generosity without self-preservation helps no one.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this decision?

options.text: Those closest to you have the first claim on your care and resources.
A community that lets people die at its gates has lost the right to call itself a community.
The answer depends on how severe the risk is. At some point generosity becomes recklessness.

scenarios.tradition_note: Graded love (ai you cha deng): ren (benevolence) radiates outward from family. You owe more to those closer to you. The Mohist counter-argument was universal love (jian ai). The dilemma: when graded love produces outcomes that feel unjust to outsiders.
scenarios.stimulus: A government official must allocate reconstruction funds after flooding damaged two regions equally. One region is his home province, where his extended family and lifelong friends live. The other region is distant and unfamiliar to him. He allocates more resources to his home province, explaining that he knows its needs best and has deeper obligations there. His critics say a public official must serve all citizens equally.

judgment.question: How do you see his decision?

options.text: His deeper knowledge of and obligation to his home community makes his decision understandable and defensible.
A public official who favors his own people over others is failing his duty to serve impartially.
His feelings are natural but his role requires him to set them aside. Public office demands impartiality.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this decision?

options.text: We inevitably know and care more about those closest to us, and that deeper connection produces better care.
Justice requires treating equal needs equally, regardless of personal connection.
The role changes the obligation. What is natural for a person is a failure for an official.

scenarios.tradition_note: Ummah (universal community of believers) creates a scope of obligation that transcends local and national boundaries but is still bounded by faith community. Zakat (obligatory charity) has specific categories of recipients. The dilemma: when universal ummah obligations and local family obligations compete.
scenarios.stimulus: A man donates generously to humanitarian relief for communities suffering overseas, where the need is clearly greater. His own extended family, while not destitute, faces financial pressures — a cousin cannot afford medical treatment, a nephew needs help with school fees. His family says charity begins at home and that he is neglecting the people God placed closest to him. He says the overseas need is more severe and that faith demands response to the greatest suffering regardless of proximity.

judgment.question: How do you see his choices?

options.text: His family has the first claim. You cannot reach across the world while stepping over your own people.
The greatest need should determine where help goes, regardless of relationship.
Both claims are real. He should find a balance rather than choosing one at the expense of the other.

reasoning.question: What matters most in evaluating his choices?

options.text: Those God placed in your life are your first responsibility. Distant charity does not excuse local neglect.
A person dying of hunger overseas does not suffer less because they are far away.
The obligation is to give. How it is divided requires wisdom, not a formula.

scenarios.tradition_note: Varnashrama dharma: obligations differ by one's role and life stage. A householder has different duties than a renunciant. The dilemma: when universal compassion (karuna) conflicts with role-specific duty.
scenarios.stimulus: A doctor in a small town has been providing free treatment to poor patients from surrounding villages, often at the expense of time with her own family and paying patients who keep her practice running. Her husband says she is neglecting her duty as a wife and mother by giving so much to strangers. She says her skill creates an obligation to use it wherever the need is greatest. He says that duty to her family is her primary dharma at this stage of life.

judgment.question: How do you see their disagreement?

options.text: Her husband is right. At this stage of life, family is her primary duty. Compassion for strangers cannot override it.
Her medical skill creates an obligation to help those in need that cannot be overridden by family convenience.
Both duties are real. She needs to find a sustainable balance, not choose one over the other.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding their disagreement?

options.text: Duty changes with life stage. A householder's primary obligation is to the household.
A healer who turns away suffering to tend to comfort has lost sight of what healing means.
The question is not which duty is primary but how to honor both without destroying either.

scenarios.tradition_note: Ubuntu obligation: 'your child is my child.' Communal responsibility for children extends beyond biological parents. The dilemma: when communal responsibility is invoked by strangers.
scenarios.stimulus: A woman living in a city receives a request from a family in her home village. Their daughter has been accepted to a school in the city but has no place to stay. They ask the woman to take the girl in for the school year. The woman has her own children and limited space. She barely knows this family but they share the same community of origin. Declining would be seen as a betrayal of the communal bonds she grew up with. Accepting would strain her own family's resources.

judgment.question: How should she respond?

options.text: The community raised her. She owes it to them to help raise the next generation, even at personal cost.
She has her own family to provide for. An obligation based on shared origins has limits.
She should try to help but negotiate terms that protect her own family's wellbeing.

reasoning.question: What matters most in this situation?

options.text: Every child in the community is everyone's responsibility. That is what community means.
Communal obligations cannot be open-ended demands on people who have their own families to support.
The obligation is real but so are the limits. Finding a way to help without breaking is the challenge.

scenarios.tradition_note: Extending ren (benevolence) beyond family: Mencius argued that moral feeling naturally extends outward (the child at the well). But the practical reality is that family bonds are strongest. The dilemma: when extending benevolence to outsiders is costly to the family.
scenarios.stimulus: A shopkeeper in a small town has been extending credit to a struggling family he knows from his neighborhood. They are honest but unable to pay. His own family's finances are now strained by the unpaid debts. His wife says his generosity to outsiders is coming at their children's expense. He says that a person who sees suffering and does nothing when he can help has failed as a human being.

judgment.question: How do you see his situation?

options.text: His first duty is to his own family. Generosity that harms your children is not virtue — it is neglect.
He is right to help. A person who only cares for his own family has a small heart.
His impulse is good but he has extended it past the point where it is sustainable.

reasoning.question: What matters most in understanding his situation?

options.text: Benevolence starts at home. A man who cannot provide for his own children cannot claim to be virtuous.
The measure of a person is how they treat those outside their own circle.
Virtue without practical wisdom leads to harm. Knowing when to stop is part of being good.

name: CMRB Consolidated Bank (48)
